newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold-Physical buyers see downside potential.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold-Physical buyers see downside potential.

text.p: Spot gold has hovered at its current US$340-$345 per ounce level long enough to convince jaded physical buyers to wait for even lower prices before purchasing, regional gold traders said on Friday.
"People got used to cheap prices and the market has not rebounded towards the upside, so physical demand is very slow," said one trader.
Singapore traders said there have been no substantial purchases from the jewellery sector and people were just marking time.
Buying interest had been exhausted at current levels but could re-emerge at $338 or $339 per ounce, Hong Kong dealers said.
Asian market sentiment saw gold dipping even further, with one senior trader predicting the possiblity of it dropping to between $330 and $335 per ounce.
In the near term, spot prices would likely be locked in a range between US$340 and $343 an ounce, dealers said.
"I doubt it will break out of its range anytime soon," one Singapore dealer said.
Funds still holding short positions had no intention of buying back at these levels and their search for lower ranges pressured the market, a senior Hong Kong dealer said.
"The market is sleepy. There's no real sense of urgency among buyers to pick up material," a dealer for a bank in Singapore said.
"This is a bad time for demand," another trader said. "People are just buying what they need. We're not seeing any accumulation across the Asia-Pacific region."
Hong Kong gold opened at US$340.30/80 per ounce on Friday, a shade below New York's $340.50/341.00 close on Thursday.
In early afternoon, gold was trading at $340.55/85 per ounce in quiet trade as Sydney markets were closed, dealers said.
"There is not much trading interest and there is nothing going on," a source said.
The market was expected to remain quiet ahead of the over-the-counter options expiry on Monday.
Singapore premiums over spot London prices were steady at 90-120 U.S. cents an ounce.

"Premiums are being shored up by routine business. But the premiums are 20-30 cents down from the peak we saw in February," one trader said, referring to premium levels of 160 U.S. cents just before the Lunar New Year holidays early this year.
